h1: Buying homebrew ingredients when there is no shop nearby
title: Buying Homebrew Ingredients Remotely | Craft Beer School
desc: How to source malt, hops, yeast and equipment by post or from local substitutes and how to keep them in good shape when delivery is slow.
teaser: No homebrew shop for 500 km? Plan an order, protect it on the journey and know which local substitutes work.
standfirst: If the nearest homebrew supplier is a long parcel journey away, the aim is to order smart: what keeps, what does not and what you can replace with what is nearby.
sections: Sort ingredients by how well they keep

Not everything in a recipe suffers in the post. Whole malt keeps for months if it is stored dry. Dry yeast keeps for months to years in the fridge and survives several days of heat. Hops are the delicate item. They lose bitterness and aroma with heat and air, so they need cold storage and vacuum packs. Liquid yeast, fresh fruit and anything damp are the worst to ship. Buy accordingly.
Build a stock list, not a shopping list

Every parcel carries its own handling and delivery charge, so order in bulk for several batches. A 25 kg sack of base malt is the cheapest way to get pale malt. Keep it in sealed buckets. Add a few kilos of speciality malts, a handful of dry yeast sachets in two or three types and sanitiser. Hops go in vacuum bags, ideally in a 100 g size, which you freeze on arrival.

A group order with other brewers is often the best solution. Share a sack of malt with three friends and the postage drops sharply. Ask on local forums or at a nearby bar.
Choose a supplier who ships to your climate

Ask the shop how they pack hops and yeast for hot destinations. Good suppliers use cool packs, insulated envelopes and a courier that does not leave parcels in a vehicle. Order in your cooler months if you can. Ask about the courier route and the likely number of days: five days in a postal system is different from fifteen.

Check your country's rules before you order. Customs and food import rules vary and can affect grain, yeast and hops. Ask the shop or your national authority.

Open the parcel the day it arrives. Put hops in the freezer. Put yeast in the fridge. Check malt for dampness or insects. Record the date. If something has spoiled in transit, photograph it for the supplier. For hot-weather storage details, see storing hops in hot weather. For the long-distance side, hop freshness across long supply chains goes into the chemistry.

Many ingredients have local alternatives. Table sugar or honey can prime bottles, though honey is less predictable. Local wheat, rice and maize can replace speciality adjuncts. Fresh fruit and local spices flavour beer well. Raw flour and grains need a cook and enough malt enzymes behind them, so keep them to a minority of the grist. Do not substitute bread yeast for beer yeast: it ferments differently and the beer shows it. A proper beer yeast is worth the postage. See choosing yeast for a warm room.
Extract and kits as a bridge

If grain is hard to find, malt extract, liquid or dry, is a legitimate way to brew. It is lighter to ship and keeps well when sealed. Extract kits give good beer with less equipment and a shorter brew day. You can later add steeped grains for flavour and move to all-grain when your supply is better. There is no shame in a good extract beer and many good brewers started that way.

Whatever the route, keep notes on what you ordered, when it arrived and how the beer turned out. Your supply is part of your recipe.

Some equipment is easy to make or find locally. A food-grade bucket with a lid makes a fermenter once you drill the lid for a grommet and airlock. A large stainless stockpot from a kitchen shop is a kettle. A nylon mesh bag from a sewing shop or a voile curtain, boiled and sanitised, is a brew bag. A cheap kitchen thermometer works, provided you check it in ice water (0 °C) and boiling water.

Do not improvise a hydrometer, which has no good substitute. Never reuse glass or plastic that once held chemicals. Sanitiser matters too, so order a good one.

The hard part of remote buying is knowing what to order. A recipe may call for a malt that your supplier has under a different name, or a yeast with several similar variants. In our class you learn how to read a malt spec sheet and how to substitute without losing the beer. That saves expensive parcels.
faqs: What should I buy in bulk when there is no shop nearby?
Base malt in a sealed container, dry yeast sachets and sanitiser. Buy hops in vacuum packs and freeze them on arrival.
Does yeast survive postal delivery in hot weather?
Dry yeast usually does. Liquid yeast is more fragile and best avoided for long, hot journeys.
Can I brew without a homebrew shop at all?
Yes. Malt extract, dry yeast and a little planning with online suppliers are enough to brew good beer.
How do I check hops arrived in good shape?
They should smell fresh and be sealed and cool. Cheesy or hay-like smells suggest age or heat damage.
